title: "Toy Simulations"

R version of `src/simulations/toy_examples.ipynb`, translation aided by Claude.
DECIDE, regression and fANOVA use the R implementations in `R/` (`decide()`,
`calc_regression()` and `calc_fanova()`); the random forests' MDI and
permutation importances come from scikit-learn via reticulate, since it allows
trees to be grown deeper and thus actually learn the small multiverse. R
versions of RF still cause MDI and PFI to get it wrong, but it is so wrong
mostly due to poor fit, which is not the point we are trying to make here.
Results are identical to the toy_examples.ipynb file.

We would like to show that our framework elegantly handles cases where
surrogate model-based decision importances fail. In particular, we consider toy
multiverses that poke holes in how regression and random forests handle
decision importances.

```{r setup}
here::i_am("toy_examples.qmd")
source(here::here("R", "_load.R"))
use_virtualenv(here::here("..", ".venv"))
sk_ensemble <- import("sklearn.ensemble")
sk_inspection <- import("sklearn.inspection")
```

## Helpers

```{r helpers}
# A toy multiverse from a 0/1 design matrix (one column per decision) and its
# outcomes, with the decisions as mv_dim_ columns
make_toy_mv <- function (X, accuracy) {
  as_tibble(X, .name_repair = "minimal") |>
    rename_with(\(name) paste0("mv_dim_", name)) |>
    mutate(accuracy = accuracy)
}

toy_design <- function (mv) {
  as.matrix(mv |> select(starts_with("mv_dim_")))
}

# DECIDE total effect per decision, in the multiverse's decision order
decide_total <- function (mv) {
  result <- decide(mv, "accuracy")
  setNames(result$decide_total, result$dimension)[colnames(toy_design(mv))]
}

# Random forest (scikit-learn defaults) importances, averaged over `seeds`: mean
# decrease in impurity (MDI) and permutation feature importance (PFI, increase
# in MSE over 50 shuffles), plus the in-sample R^2
rf_importances <- function (mv, seeds, bootstrap = TRUE) {
  X <- toy_design(mv)
  y <- mv$accuracy
  runs <- lapply(seeds, function (seed) {
    rf <- sk_ensemble$RandomForestRegressor(random_state = as.integer(seed), bootstrap = bootstrap)
    rf$fit(X, y)
    pfi <- sk_inspection$permutation_importance(
      rf, X, y, n_repeats = 50L, random_state = as.integer(seed),
      scoring = "neg_mean_squared_error"
    )
    predictions <- as.numeric(rf$predict(X))
    list(
      mdi = setNames(as.numeric(rf$feature_importances_), colnames(X)),
      pfi = setNames(as.numeric(pfi$importances_mean), colnames(X)),
      r2 = 1 - sum((y - predictions)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2),
      predictions = predictions
    )
  })
  list(
    mdi = do.call(rbind, lapply(runs, \(run) run$mdi)),
    pfi = do.call(rbind, lapply(runs, \(run) run$pfi)),
    r2 = mean(vapply(runs, \(run) run$r2, numeric(1))),
    predictions = rowMeans(sapply(runs, \(run) run$predictions))
  )
}

# fANOVA main effects (each decision on its own) and total effects (main effect
# plus every interaction the decision is part of), averaged over `seeds`.
# Further arguments go to the fANOVA forest (see calc_fanova()).
fanova_main_total <- function (mv, seeds, ...) {
  runs <- lapply(seeds, function (seed) {
    # (quiet: calc_fanova() reads its results back with an unnamed index column)
    components <- suppressMessages(
      calc_fanova(mv, "accuracy", use_individual = FALSE, seed = seed, ...)
    )
    level_cols <- grep("^level_", colnames(components), value = TRUE)
    main <- components |>
      filter(if_all(all_of(setdiff(level_cols, "level_0")), is.na)) |>
      select(decision = level_0, main = individual_importance)
    total <- fanova_total_to_vec(components) |>
      enframe(name = "decision", value = "total")
    left_join(main, total, by = "decision")
  })
  bind_rows(runs) |>
    group_by(decision) |>
    summarise(main = mean(main), total = mean(total), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(match(decision, colnames(toy_design(mv))))
}
```

# Toy Multiverse #1

**Regression predictions fail; RF predictions succeed; MDI importances fail;
permutation importances succeed.**

Interactions can cause linear regression models to fail both in prediction and
interpretation, assuming that the interaction terms are not all included. If
the interaction terms are all included, this can also lead to the case where
$p = n$, so the regression will perfectly interpolate the data, but the model
will have zero residual degrees of freedom, making statistical inference
impossible (i.e. no standard errors or p-values can be calculated). Thus the
only way around this problem is to know the interactions in advance, which is
infeasible for large/complex multiverses.

Since random forests are ensembles of rule-based models, they handle the
multiverses with a high amount of accuracy. In fact, if we set
`bootstrap = False` (since we observe the full multiverse), then it will often
get perfect predictive accuracy. However, MDI importances, which are the most
popular form of tree-based importance, will fail. This is because for each
possible initial split in a tree, each candidate feature yields a variance
reduction of exactly 0, so the root node will get nothing. The tree is forced to
arbitrarily pick one of the features to serve as the root node, and assuming it
chooses `x1`, then `x1` will not receive any credit. However, if the researcher
is savvy enough to know this is a potential issue, then permutation importance
can be used and will sidestep this issue.

```{r toy1-multiverse}
toy1_X <- cbind(
  x1 = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1),
  x2 = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1),
  x3 = c(0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1)
)
mv_toy1 <- make_toy_mv(toy1_X, c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6))
mv_toy1
```

## Regression

```{r toy1-regression}
reg_toy1 <- calc_regression(mv_toy1, "accuracy")
coef(reg_toy1)
cat("R^2:", summary(reg_toy1)$r.squared, "\n")
cat("Predictions:", fitted(reg_toy1), "\n")
```

Including every interaction fits the data perfectly, but leaves no residual
degrees of freedom:

```{r toy1-regression-saturated}
reg_toy1_full <- lm(accuracy ~ (mv_dim_x1 + mv_dim_x2 + mv_dim_x3)^3, data = mv_toy1)
coef(reg_toy1_full)
cat("n =", nrow(mv_toy1), " p =", length(coef(reg_toy1_full)),
    " residual df =", df.residual(reg_toy1_full), "\n")
cat("R^2:", summary(reg_toy1_full)$r.squared, "\n")
```

## Random forest

```{r toy1-random-forest}
rf_toy1 <- rf_importances(mv_toy1, seeds = 42)
rf_toy1[c("mdi", "pfi", "r2")]
cat("Predictions:", round(rf_toy1$predictions, 3), "\n")

rf_toy1_nb <- rf_importances(mv_toy1, seeds = 42, bootstrap = FALSE)
rf_toy1_nb[c("mdi", "pfi", "r2")]
cat("Predictions (no bootstrap):", round(rf_toy1_nb$predictions, 3), "\n")
```

## fANOVA

```{r toy1-fanova}
fanova_main_total(mv_toy1, seeds = 42)
```

## DECIDE

```{r toy1-decide}
decide_total(mv_toy1)
```

# Counterexample Construction

We discuss here how to create a multiverse such that regression, standard
tree-based importances, and fANOVA all fail. Split the judgment calls into two
groups:

1. An interaction: these decisions affect the outcome only through a joint
   interaction among themselves (their parity, in our case), so every one of
   them has a main effect of exactly zero.
2. One main-effect decision: this decision impacts the results through a pure
   main effect and participates in no interactions.

The importances have to be such that the interaction is more important than the
main effect. This means each decision in the interaction must move the outcome
more than the main-effect decision does in every background context. Every
surrogate-based importance then fails, putting the main-effect decision before
the decisions comprising the interaction:

- Linear regression can only see main effects unless the analyst names the
  right interaction terms in advance, so the interacting group receives
  coefficients of zero. Naming all the interactions instead saturates the model
  ($p = n$) and destroys inference.
- MDI is greedy. Splitting on any single member of the interacting group
  reduces impurity by exactly zero, so the group's contribution is only paid
  out deep in the tree, and is then divided among its members. The main effect
  is in a single split at the root and is credited to one decision.
- Permutation importance measures how much a decision impacts the forest's
  predictions. Thus, if the model doesn't properly learn the multiverse
  structure, it doesn't have the right idea of decision importances.
- fANOVA also relies on the forest's predictions, and thus has the same
  drawback as permutation importance.

How much this setup breaks the above methods is dictated by the number of
decisions in the interacting group: the more decisions, the more wrong
permutation importance and fANOVA become. Toy #2 uses four interacting
decisions, the minimal version below uses two.

# Toy Multiverse #2

**Regression fails; RF predictions fail; MDI importances fail; permutation
importances fail.**

Decisions `s1`--`s4` act on accuracy only through their joint (four-way)
interaction: accuracy is high when an even number of them are set to 1 and low
otherwise, so each of them has a main effect of exactly zero. Decision `s5`
acts through a main effect with no interactions. `s1`--`s4` matter strictly
more than `s5` in every universe: switching any one of `s1`--`s4` moves accuracy
by 0.06, whereas switching `s5` moves it by 0.04.

Permutation importance fails because of bagging. With bootstrapping (the
default in every package) each universe is out-of-bag for roughly 37% of the
trees. A tree that has the universe in-bag reproduces its accuracy exactly; a
tree that does not has to predict it from neighbouring universes, and for a
pure interaction those neighbours carry no information about it.

```{r toy2-multiverse}
# balanced / full factorial: 2^5 = 32 universes, in the same order as Python's
# itertools.product (first decision varies slowest)
toy2_X <- as.matrix(expand_grid(s1 = 0:1, s2 = 0:1, s3 = 0:1, s4 = 0:1, s5 = 0:1))
# accuracy is BASE +/- A according to the parity of s1..s4, plus a flat D for s5
BASE <- 0.80; A <- 0.03; D <- 0.04
mv_toy2 <- make_toy_mv(toy2_X, BASE + A * (-1)^rowSums(toy2_X[, 1:4]) + D * toy2_X[, 5])
cat("n universes:", nrow(mv_toy2), "\n")
cat("distinct accuracies:", sort(unique(mv_toy2$accuracy)), "\n")
```

## DECIDE

The total effect ranks `s1`--`s4` above `s5`, by the correct factor of 2.25:

```{r toy2-decide}
decide_total(mv_toy2)
```

## Regression

The four interacting decisions get coefficients of exactly zero:

```{r toy2-regression}
reg_toy2 <- calc_regression(mv_toy2, "accuracy")
round(coef(reg_toy2), 5)
cat("R^2:", summary(reg_toy2)$r.squared, "\n")
```

Including every interaction restores the fit but leaves no residual degrees of
freedom:

```{r toy2-regression-saturated}
reg_toy2_full <- lm(accuracy ~ (mv_dim_s1 + mv_dim_s2 + mv_dim_s3 + mv_dim_s4 + mv_dim_s5)^5, data = mv_toy2)
cat("n =", nrow(mv_toy2), " p =", length(coef(reg_toy2_full)),
    " residual df =", df.residual(reg_toy2_full), "\n")
cat("R^2:", summary(reg_toy2_full)$r.squared, "\n")
```

## Random forest

Averaged over 10 seeds, so the conclusion does not rest on tie-breaking:

```{r toy2-random-forest}
rf_toy2 <- rf_importances(mv_toy2, seeds = 0:9)
round(rbind(MDI = colMeans(rf_toy2$mdi), PFI = colMeans(rf_toy2$pfi)), 5)
cat("seeds where s5 outranks all of s1-s4: MDI",
    sum(rf_toy2$mdi[, 5] > apply(rf_toy2$mdi[, 1:4], 1, max)), "/ 10, PFI",
    sum(rf_toy2$pfi[, 5] > apply(rf_toy2$pfi[, 1:4], 1, max)), "/ 10\n")
```

## fANOVA

```{r toy2-fanova}
fanova_main_total(mv_toy2, seeds = 42)
```

# A Minimal Version

- `s1` and `s2` act only through their pairwise interaction.
- `s3` is a pure main effect.

Switching `s1` or `s2` moves accuracy by 0.05 in every background context,
switching `s3` moves it by 0.04. This is the multiverse in Section 4 of the
paper (Figure 4 and Table 1).

```{r minimal-multiverse}
min_X <- as.matrix(expand_grid(s1 = 0:1, s2 = 0:1, s3 = 0:1))
MIN_BASE <- 0.80; MIN_A <- 0.025; MIN_D <- 0.04
mv_min <- make_toy_mv(min_X, MIN_BASE + MIN_A * (-1)^rowSums(min_X[, 1:2]) + MIN_D * min_X[, 3])
mv_min
```

## DECIDE

```{r minimal-decide}
decide_min <- decide_total(mv_min)
decide_min
```

## Regression

```{r minimal-regression}
reg_min <- calc_regression_importance(mv_min, "accuracy")[paste0("mv_dim_", colnames(min_X))]
round(reg_min, 5)
cat("R^2:", summary(calc_regression(mv_min, "accuracy"))$r.squared, "\n")
```

## Random forest

```{r minimal-random-forest}
rf_min <- rf_importances(mv_min, seeds = 0:9)
round(rbind(MDI = colMeans(rf_min$mdi), PFI = colMeans(rf_min$pfi)), 5)

rf_min_nb <- rf_importances(mv_min, seeds = 0:9, bootstrap = FALSE)
round(rbind(MDI = colMeans(rf_min_nb$mdi), PFI = colMeans(rf_min_nb$pfi)), 5)
```

## fANOVA

With the `fanova` package's default forest (a bootstrap sample per tree, 70% of
the decisions considered at each split), averaged over 10 seeds:

```{r minimal-fanova}
fanova_min <- fanova_main_total(mv_min, seeds = 0:9)
fanova_min
```

With an interpolating forest (no bootstrapping, every decision considered at
each split), fANOVA's total effects recover DECIDE's ranking (as shares of the
total variance), while its main effects still give the interacting decisions
nothing:

```{r minimal-fanova-interpolated}
fanova_main_total(mv_min, seeds = 0:9, bootstrapping = FALSE, max_features = ncol(min_X))
decide_min / pop_var(mv_min$accuracy)
```

## Table 1

The importances of every method on the minimal multiverse, with the most
important decision(s) per method in bold, as written to
`tables/toy-importance-comparison.tex`:

```{r minimal-table}
toy_table <- tibble(
  decision = c("$c_1$", "$c_2$", "$c_3$"),
  decide_total = unname(decide_min),
  regression = unname(reg_min),
  fanova_main = fanova_min$main,
  fanova_total = fanova_min$total,
  mdi = unname(colMeans(rf_min$mdi)),
  pfi = unname(colMeans(rf_min$pfi))
) |>
  # bold the most important decision(s) per column (ties are all bolded)
  mutate(across(-decision, \(values) if_else(
    abs(values - max(values)) <= 1e-9 * abs(max(values)),
    sprintf("\\textbf{%.6f}", values),
    sprintf("%.6f", values)
  )))

toy_kbl <- knitr::kable(
  toy_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  linesep = "",
  align = c("l", rep("c", 6)),
  caption = paste(
    "Comparison of decision importance scores on the multiverse shown in",
    "Figure~\\ref{fig:mv-proxy-counterexample}. Only $\\method_\\texttt{total}$",
    "correctly identifies that the interacting decisions ($c_1, c_2$) have a",
    "higher importance than the main effect decision ($c_3$)."
  ),
  label = "toy-importance-comparison",
  col.names = c("", "$\\method_{\\texttt{total}}$", "Reg.", "Main", "Total", "MDI", "PFI")
) |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 3, "fANOVA" = 2, "Random Forest" = 2))

cat(as.character(toy_kbl))

tables_dir <- here::here("tables")
if (!dir.exists(tables_dir)) dir.create(tables_dir, recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(as.character(toy_kbl), file.path(tables_dir, "toy-importance-comparison.tex"))
```

# Notes

## Permutation importance without bootstrapping

If we turn bagging off, permutation importance works perfectly here. This will
always be true, since a fully-grown, non-bootstrapped forest interpolates the
multiverse, so its predictions for each permuted row witness the change in the
true accuracy. Writing $p_{-i}$ for the background context and $s_i, s_i'$ for
two independent draws of decision $i$, the mean-squared-error permutation
importance is

$$
PFI(i) = \mathbb{E}\left[\left(f(s_i, p_{-i}) - f(s_i', p_{-i})\right)^2\right]
= 2\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{-i}}\left[\mathrm{Var}_{s_i}(f)\right]
= 2 \cdot \mathrm{DECIDE}(i),
$$

up to an $O(1/n)$ correction from permuting without replacement. Permutation
importance and the DECIDE total effect are then the same statistic up to a
factor of two.

## Connections to fANOVA

fANOVA also fails, and does so worse than permutation importance. This is
because **fANOVA is the DECIDE decomposition of the forest's predictions rather
than of the multiverse.** Its total importance for decision $i$ is
$\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\hat f \mid X_{-i})]$, the total effect of $i$
evaluated on $\hat f$ instead of $f$. Thus, if the surrogate model is wrong,
fANOVA is also wrong. Unlike permutation importance, which is scored against
the true outcomes and thus can partially recover, fANOVA never looks at the
true outcomes once the forest is fit.

Turning off bootstrapping is not enough to fix the method, because `fanova`
also sets `max_features = (n_features * 7) // 10`: only 70% of the decisions
are considered at each split, which on its own prevents the forest from
reconstructing a high-order interaction. Any surrogate randomization that stops
the forest from interpolating produces this failure.

When fANOVA does interpolate (setting `max_features` to the number of
decisions), it returns rescaled DECIDE importances. This is the same collapse
we saw for permutation importance: on a balanced multiverse, fANOVA on an
interpolating surrogate is DECIDE, computed the expensive way through a model
that can only lose information.
